skyline.text: Why Amit Varma stood up for a podcaster nobody would defend
Ajay Shah on why an infirm state calls for fewer curbs
Why every right flows from a newborn owning itself

footnote.text: The right to free speech is absolute.

brief.head: Over to the bench
brief.text: People who want black-and-white laws on incitement, Ajay Shah said, are not respecting the common law, where judges read subtle cases and draw the line. {088-C08}

brief.head: Blocked, not banned
brief.text: Blocking someone on Twitter is not censorship, Amit Varma said: no one is entitled to your attention. The battle for free speech is against the state. {088-C09}

brief.head: Rumour control
brief.text: The government has forced companies to watch social media and rebut rumours about them. That is “just dumb”, Ajay Shah said: a firm should be busy doing its business. {088-J18}

brief.head: Snowflake nation
brief.text: Why watch a show you dislike? Get a life, Ajay Shah said. India has a snowflakes problem, he argued: people so insecure that mere words wound them. {#snowflakes}

brief.head: Mature enough
brief.text: To those who say Indians are too sensitive for free speech, Amit Varma replied that India has negotiated greater diversity than any other part of the world, for centuries. {#meltingpot}

thought.who: Amit Varma, on what a case under Section 295A costs the accused, whatever the verdict

lead.kicker: Amit Varma makes the case for free speech absolutism
lead.head: No shades of grey on speech
body: Amit Varma says he is all shades of grey on facts, because the world is too complicated to understand in its entirety. On certain values he is black and white, and free speech is one of them. {088-C01}
“I am a free speech absolutist,” he said, and with Ajay Shah he set out what that means and how it has fared in India.
## What set it off

The episode was topical, a rarity for a show that aims to be timeless. The podcaster Ranveer Allahbadia had asked a crude question about parents and incest on *India’s Got Latent*, a subscription-only comedy show on YouTube.

A clip went viral, the right piled on, and then the state stepped in: police cases, a passport taken away, an order to produce no more content. Around forty people connected to the show faced cases, including the editor.
Varma, who has never watched a full episode of Allahbadia’s show, tweeted that he was a well-intentioned kid who had apologised gracefully. Left and right both came down on Varma.
“A fundamental principle of free speech is you should defend the people that you disagree with the most,” he said. {088-S02}
His fear is that a hated target lets the state bring in a broadcast bill through the back door, or simply normalise treating creators this way.
## Three arguments

Varma’s first argument comes from first principles. Following John Locke, a newborn child owns itself, not the king or the state, and every right flows from that. Silence someone and you deny their personhood and agency.
The second is the marketplace of ideas, where ideas compete and, in Matt Ridley’s phrase, have sex. An official view can be wrong, and progress, Varma said, comes from heretics.
The third is democracy, a contest of ideas about how to run a country. Punish one person’s speech and others think twice: electoral manipulation without touching a ballot box.
## A constable’s Constitution

India, Varma argued, never enshrined free speech at all. Article 19(1)(a) grants it; Article 19(2) at once allows “reasonable restrictions” on vague grounds such as public order, decency and morality.
Who interprets them? The police constable, he said, recalling Somnath Lahiri’s protest in the constituent assembly that fundamental rights had been framed from a constable’s point of view. {088-C04}
That is why colonial-era laws such as 295A, 153A and the sedition law, 124A, survive in India, though they no longer exist in Britain.

When sedition was struck down in the early 1950s, Jawaharlal Nehru answered with the First Amendment. {088-S04} Syama Prasad Mookerjee asked him what precedent he was laying down if “some other party comes into authority”.
The elites, Varma said, fail in two ways. They infantilise citizens, and they are hypocrites, condemning speech laws used against their side and cheering when those laws hit their enemies. {088-C06}
To the standard objections he had answers. Falsely shouting fire in a crowded theatre is already trespass and harm; if hate speech leads to violence, punish the violence.
His line is America’s: all speech, hate speech included, short of direct incitement to violence. “Here is Ajay Shah’s address, go and lynch him” is where it is crossed.

Shah, closing, pushed the case further. Because filing a case in India is itself the punishment, he argued, the country needs “even lower restrictions on free speech” than countries such as the UK, not the same.

second.label: Art and provocation
second.head: Verses yes, cartoons no?
second.deck: Amit Varma rejects an MP’s line between a novel and a cartoon
body: Around 2007 or 2008, during the violence over the Danish cartoons, a man Amit Varma calls perhaps the most sensible MP in the country today wrote a column. Varma would not name him. {088-S07}
The MP said he supported Salman Rushdie and *The Satanic Verses*, but not the Danish cartoonists. {#rushdie} The novel, he argued, was a work of art; the cartoons were mere provocation.

Varma rejects the distinction. You might like the novel and find the cartoons obnoxious and repulsive, he said, but both have an equal right to free speech. Such hypocrisy, he added, is rampant around us today.

quote.text: They’re absolutely equal. If you’re going by principle, you have to support both.

photo.hint: novelist, author of The Satanic Verses

second.caption: art versus provocation

third.head: Moved by the moving image
body: In 1968 K.A. Abbas made *A Tale of Four Cities*, a documentary set in Mumbai’s red-light districts. It was objected to, and the matter went all the way to the Supreme Court.

The court ruled that cinema needed closer scrutiny than the written word. Amit Varma read from the judgment: “a person reading a book or other writing or hearing a speech or viewing a painting or sculpture is not so deeply stirred as by seeing a motion picture.” {088-S05}
That reasoning, Varma said, is why film censorship exists: a board of bureaucrats decides what is fit for Indian society, because people are thought so impressionable. {#board}
“We have normalised it, we take it for granted,” he said, calling it “such a deeply objectionable way of thinking”.

p2.title: Speak, and let speak
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s case for free speech absolutism, chapter by chapter, with Ajay Shah’s twist at the end

sections.label: Three arguments
sections.head: Let a hundred heretics bloom
sections.caption: the three arguments for free speech
body: Amit Varma has been writing columns on free speech for more than twenty years. {#columns} He laid out the three big arguments he has made through all of them.
The first is from first principles, and runs through John Locke. When a newborn child is born, who owns it? Not society, not the state, not a king. A child owns itself. {#locke}

From that right to self-ownership flow the others: to life, to property, and to free expression, because your thoughts are your own. To silence someone, Varma said, is to deny their personhood and agency, and an attack on one person’s agency is an attack on everybody’s.
## Ideas in the marketplace
The next two arguments come from consequences. In a free marketplace of ideas, ideas compete and recombine, or, in Matt Ridley’s phrase, ideas have sex, and the best ones come to the fore. {088-R08}
If the state prescribes one view of the world, that view may be wrong. You should be free to say the earth goes around the sun, Varma said, and equally free to say the opposite. {088-C03}

~ The third argument is democracy, which Varma defined as a competition between different points of view about the best way to run a country. Punish one person’s speech, he said, and tomorrow others will think twice before saying the same thing. That chilling effect is electoral manipulation without a rigged booth. {#chilling}

quote.text: Progress comes from heretics. Progress comes from people saying that the earth goes around the sun and not vice versa

sections.label: The history
sections.head: Constitution, now a periodical
sections.caption: India’s troubled history of free speech
body: For Amit Varma, the gold standard of free speech is the US First Amendment: “Congress shall make no law” abridging the freedom of speech or of the press. No caveats, no exceptions. {#gold}

India’s Constitution is another matter. Drawing on Subhashish Bhadra’s *Caged Tiger*, Varma said constitutions are products of their circumstances. {088-R05} India’s was framed amid turmoil, with more than five hundred princely states, so it centralised power and paid lip service to freedom.
India, Varma said, exchanged white-skinned rulers for brown-skinned ones: the colonial state, built to rule subjects rather than serve citizens, was adopted wholesale.
## Lacking a theory of the state

Ajay Shah would not fault the individuals in the constituent assembly, who represented the intellectual capital of India. “But I think that they were just lacking in their understanding of the state,” he said. {#theory}

Leaders from Nehru and Indira onwards amended the Constitution so often to do unconstitutional things, Varma said, that a cartoon of the time had a parliament bookstore clerk explain that he did not stock periodicals. {088-J09}
~ Varma recalled that in the early 1950s even Ambedkar, once proud of the Constitution, said he would gladly burn it himself. {088-J17}

quote.text: I feel that many of these fundamental rights have been framed from the point of view of a police constable.
quote.who: Somnath Lahiri, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The elites
sections.head: The masses are not the problem
sections.caption: infantilisation and hypocrisy
body: Power corrupts character, Amit Varma said, and not just in the obvious sense of wanting more money. The founding generation were the best and brightest, but proximity to power bred arrogance. {088-C05}
He named two failings of the elites. The first is infantilisation: treating citizens as incapable of deciding for themselves. Film censorship came out of exactly that thinking.

Varma was recently on a podcast co-hosted by a former guest of *The Seen and the Unseen* who is close to the Congress party. She said we need to uplift the consciousness of the masses. Varma’s reply: “No, masses are not the problem, you are the problem.” {088-S08}
## Laws for thee

The second failing is hypocrisy. A prominent figure on the left told Varma that 295A and 153A were bad laws, then in the same breath suggested to a colleague filing a 295A case against a right-wing politician.
“If you agree it is bad, it is bad, period,” Varma said. “You can’t say that don’t use it against us, but I will use it against the enemy.” {088-S06}

~ His advice for any free speech controversy: don’t personalise it, don’t politicise it. Who decides what is offensive? Today it may be your friend, tomorrow your enemy, he said, and the best way past that is to be an absolutist. {088-C02}

quote.text: Many people who claim to be for free speech are actually for free speech they agree with.

sections.label: The objections
sections.head: Punish the act, not the word
sections.caption: the standard objections
body: Ajay Shah asked Amit Varma to take on the canonical cases where speech is said to cause harm. Varma began with the cliché of falsely shouting fire in a crowded theatre, a line from Oliver Wendell Holmes in 1919 in a judgment later overturned. {#holmes}
The law should punish it, Varma said, but it has nothing to do with free speech. The shouter trespasses on the owner’s property, and causes or attempts harm to others.
Hurt feelings he dismissed: they are subjective and could cover anything. “We are adults,” he said, not kindergarten children asking teacher to take away someone’s tiffin box. {088-J11}
## Where the line falls
If hate speech leads to violence, punish the violence, and the speaker too as an accessory, but only if there was direct incitement. {088-C07}

Shah tested the line with a tweet ordering Varma’s 100,000 followers to dunk a glass of cold water on the head of Nomsita, who edits the show. Being wise and sensible, they would know it was humour. Telling the two apart, Shah said, is what common-law judges are for. {088-J07}
~ Libel belongs in civil courts, Varma said, and fraud is fraud, not speech. Shah’s example: a medicine that claims 100mg of salicylic acid and contains 50mg. {#fraud}

quote.text: If someone commits violence because of something I say, you catch that person and you punish the violence

sections.label: Ajay’s word
sections.head: Weak state, strong speech
sections.caption: why India needs freer speech
body: Ajay Shah added a layer the usual debates leave out: state capability. What works in Germany or the UK cannot be mechanically transplanted to India.

Filing a criminal or civil case and going through the courts is itself the punishment, he said, and police, prosecutors and judges do not work well. So India needs even lower restrictions on free speech than the West, not the same. {088-C10}
That should hold, Shah said, for the next hundred years, while India is still figuring out the basics of how to be a democracy.
## A market in opinions
Truth, Shah argued, is too high a bar for speech. Most of the world is a fog of war, and if you could speak only with documentary proof, you would hardly speak at all.

Securities and derivatives markets are pure marketplaces of opinion. A short seller who bets against a company and then publishes damaging claims puts his money where his mouth is, and deserves more respect than a random YouTuber dissing Infosys. {088-C11}

~ Finally, crediting their friend Suyash Rai, Shah said every medium of propaganda, from Mussolini’s radio to LLMs, has a learning curve. People once believed everything on WhatsApp; today nobody does. Let these things play out, he said, rather than use state power. {088-C12}

quote.text: You need even lower restrictions on free speech in India because of the infirmities of the state.

side.boxText: Tripurdaman Singh’s *Sixteen Stormy Days* tells the story of the First Amendment, the episode that hobbled free speech in India’s Constitution. Amit Varma calls it brilliant and says everyone should read it. Singh also discussed it on Varma’s podcast. {088-R01}

contQuote.text: Whether or not we like the people in power at one particular point in time. The only way to safeguard a democracy is through free speech.

stories.start: Now recently what happened was he went on the show called India's Got Latent
stories.end: The right to free speech involves us all, and it is above everything
stories.caption: the Ranveer Allahbadia affair
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why he defended a podcaster he does not watch
stories.head: Stand by the man you can’t stand
body: Ranveer Allahbadia, the podcaster known as BeerBiceps, runs a madly popular show. Amit Varma has never watched a full episode, but sees him as a sincere young man, curious and no kind of winger, left or right.

Then he went on *India’s Got Latent*, a subscription-only YouTube show started by the edgy comedian Samay, and asked a crude question about incest and parents. It was not even original, Varma said: an old Reddit question, used by a much bigger comedian seven years before.

A subscriber put a clip online. It went madly viral, the right wing jumped on it, and then the state got involved: police cases in several places including Assam, a passport taken away, an order to produce no more content.

Around forty people connected with the show faced cases, including the editor. An editor cuts things out, Varma noted, but cut everything objectionable from a comedy show and nothing is left. {088-J05}

Varma jumped into the fray. He tweeted that Allahbadia was a well-intentioned kid who had apologised gracefully, and that anyone who did not like the show should not watch it. {088-S02} Both left and right came down on him equally hard.

He was defending not the joke, nor even the man, he said, but the right. And Hanlon’s razor applied: never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity, or here perhaps ignorance. {088-J15}
~ Nobody has reason to defend Allahbadia, which is the danger. A hated target lets the state slip a broadcast bill through the back door, or normalise treating creators this way.
stories.why: When everybody is beating up a guy, Varma said, that is the time to speak for him. Free speech is tested by the people nobody wants to defend, since tools normalised against them can later reach anyone.
stories.postscript: Varma sometimes jokingly calls him Tequila Triceps, after the fitness channel Allahbadia first tried.

stories.start: And an interesting thing happened in the early 50s. The sedition law was struck
stories.end: some other party comes into authority, what is the precedent you are laying down?
stories.caption: Nehru and the First Amendment
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Nehru and the First Amendment
stories.head: Amend first, ask questions later
body: In the early 1950s, Jawaharlal Nehru was cracking down on speech, from the RSS magazine *The Organiser* to Romesh Thapar’s communist magazine *Crossroads*. The Supreme Court overturned the ban on *Crossroads*, and the sedition law, 124A, was struck down. {088-S04}

Nehru’s answer was the First Amendment, adding caveats such as public order and relations with friendly countries. If the courts came in the way of the legislature on basic social matters, he argued, it was for the legislature to amend the Constitution. {#nehru}

Opposition came even from people he respected: Acharya Kripalani, Jayaprakash Narayan and Syama Prasad Mookerjee. Naziruddin Ahmad, an MP from Bengal, warned that sedition would come back. It did, on the grounds the amendment laid.
~ Amit Varma admits he once wrongly said the amendment itself revived sedition, and was corrected. In spirit, he maintains, it was true.
stories.why: Even a celebrated liberal, sure that people like him will use power wisely, builds tools his rivals later inherit. Today, Varma said, the boot is on the other foot, and every party in power uses these laws.

stories.start: One that is used often against people is 295A. Deliberate uh deliberate and malicious
stories.end: et cetera, et cetera. You know the process is a punishment
stories.caption: Section 295A
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a law against outraging religious feelings
stories.head: Beef, a wedding and a joke book
body: Section 295A punishes deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings. Around 2007, Amit Varma wrote a column on how it was being used. {088-S03}

Ravi Shastri, during cricket commentary in a series in South Africa, said he likes eating beef. {#shastri} A 295A case was filed. Elizabeth Hurley married Arun Nayar without, apparently, all the Hindu rituals. Another case. The publisher of a Santa-Banta joke book got one too.
The law can be read any way you like, Varma said, and a case can be filed anywhere. If it is filed in Tripura, you have to go to the court there.
~ Its cousins are no better. Section 153A covers acts prejudicial to harmony between religious, racial, language or regional groups, and under it, Varma said, anything can be made to fit.
stories.why: Vague speech laws do their damage through the process itself, whatever the verdict. Anyone can be dragged across the country over a remark about beef, a wedding or a joke, which is why Varma calls the process a punishment.

stories.start: our good uh friend Roshan Ubbas, in fact at a party at your house
stories.end: Immediately the left jumped on him and labelled him as a right winger
stories.caption: the Aghori Baba episode
stories.kicker: Roshan Abbas’s party story, as Amit Varma retold it
stories.head: Priyanka flopped, the baba boomed
body: At a party at Ajay Shah’s house, their friend Roshan Abbas told the hosts a story about Ranveer Allahbadia. One week the podcaster released an interview with Priyanka Chopra that he thought would go madly viral. Nothing happened.
Then he put out an episode with an Aghori Baba. It got two million views in six hours, or thereabouts, and he embraced tantra and Aghori content. {088-S01}

Before the elections, government ministers including Jaishankar and Piyush Goyal skipped the smaller right-wing podcasts and went on his show. “Modiji completely ignored those guys, just went for the numbers,” Amit Varma said. {088-J04}
~ The left promptly branded Allahbadia a right-winger. He was no kind of winger, Varma said: just a curious host whose big guests asked to come on.
stories.why: Creators and politicians alike follow the numbers. Labels are often pinned on a host for who appears on the show, not for anything he believes: that is how a podcaster with no ideology became a target for both sides.

quiz.q: Which video, as Roshan Abbas told it, drew two million views in six hours for Ranveer Allahbadia?

quiz.q: Why was a 295A case filed against Ravi Shastri, as Amit Varma recalled from 2007?
quiz.a: He said on air, during a series in South Africa, that he likes eating beef.

quiz.q: Whose words did Varma borrow to say fundamental rights were framed from a police constable’s point of view?
quiz.a: Somnath Lahiri’s, spoken in protest during the constituent assembly debates.

quiz.q: What did the Supreme Court say about films in the case over K.A. Abbas’s 1968 documentary?
quiz.a: That a motion picture stirs people more deeply than a book, so needs closer scrutiny.

quiz.q: If hate speech leads someone to violence, whom does Varma say the law should punish?
quiz.a: The person who commits violence; the speaker only if he directly incited it.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, does India need even fewer curbs on speech than the West?
quiz.a: Because the state is weak: filing a case and going through courts is itself punishment.
